Research results · eleven asset classes · 1, 3 and 12 months

Can machine learning predict asset-class returns?

Can machine learning forecast the excess return over T-bills of eleven asset classes, as a full predictive distribution, better than each asset's own historical average, out of sample? This page reports what the frozen models did, how sure we can be, and what they say now.

VerdictForecast nowMean evidenceDistributionCovariancePortfolio testMethod and data
Holdout resultsHeadline figures are for forecasts made from 2015-01 on, scored once after the model lists were frozen. Development-period figures appear as context.
Verdict · Holdout (origins from 2015-01)

No mean forecast beats the historical mean at any horizon once the search over models is allowed for. The distribution forecasts score better than a volatility-tracking baseline, but not significantly once the search over models is allowed for. Dynamic covariance forecasts beat static shrinkage of the covariance at 1, 3 and 12 months. In the portfolio test, no gain from the return forecasts survives multiple-testing adjustment.

    When was any edge earned or lost?

    Cumulative squared error of the historical mean minus that of the model (the Goyal-Welch plot). The line rises in months the model was closer and falls when it was further away; a line ending above zero means the model won over the whole sample.

    Stability across periods

    Pooled out-of-sample R² by period of forecast origin.
    Evidence · predictive distribution

    Do the distribution forecasts beat a volatility baseline?

    The fair bar for a distribution forecast is not the historical mean, whose width never changes, but a forecast that simply tracks recent volatility (the EWMA volatility baseline). Beating the historical mean on CRPS mostly means tracking volatility; beating the volatility baseline means adding something to it.
